Issued at 204 PM CDT Thu Oct 22 2026

With an upper-level ridge overhead allowing a warm airmass to sit 
overhead, abnormally warm temperatures will continue today and into 
Friday. 850mb temperatures will range from the mid to upper teens 
Celsius, above the 90th percentile for this time of year. This 
translates to highs in the upper 70s to low 80s, which will approach 
daily high records. 

Southerly winds are increasing today due to a tightening pressure 
gradient, and gusts will reach up to 20-30 miles per hour over much 
of the forecast area this afternoon. The strongest gusts are 
expected over parts of central and north central South Dakota, where 
gusts up to 35 miles per hour will be possible. These winds will 
help to create some elevated fire weather concerns over parts of 
central and north central South Dakota this afternoon, with 
Grassland Fire Danger reaching the High category. 

Winds will increase further on Friday due to a low-level jet moving 
up into the region, located over eastern South Dakota and western 
Minnesota by the afternoon. The low-level jet is expected to reach 
about 40-50 knots at 850mb, but the warm air advected into the 
region at that level will help sustain a warm nose aloft. Therefore, 
those strongest gusts will likely have trouble mixing to the 
surface. Still, probabilities to hit 45 mile per hour reach between 
10-30% over much of northeastern South Dakota (with an isolated area 
up to 40%). With this in mind, confidence is not high enough for a 
headline at this time, but a close eye will be kept on observations 
through the event. As the low-level jet moves in, some scattered 
rain showers will be possible over northeastern South Dakota and 
western Minnesota. Little accumulation is expected out of these 
showers. The strong winds will also push Grassland Fire Danger 
Friday afternoon up to the High category across the forecast area, 
and even a few areas of Very High possible. The southerly winds will 
advect moisture into the region over the next couple of days, 
bringing dew points up into the mid-50s. It is this moisture that 
will keep minimum afternoon humidity between 35-50 percent and out 
of Red Flag Warning Status. 

A cold front is set to move through the region Saturday. Out ahead 
of the front, showers will develop, mainly over northeastern South 
Dakota and western Minnesota. Guidance has shown somewhat of a 
easterly shift in the extent of the precipitation in the latest 
forecast cycle. Therefore, probabilities have taken a bit of a dip, 
and chances of a tenth of an inch are down to 10-30% in that area. 
Even chances for measurable precipitation have fallen below 50% for 
most of the forecast area. Directly behind the front, winds turn 
northwesterly and increase. Gusts over central and north central 
South Dakota have a 30-50% chance to reach or exceed Wind Advisory 
criteria of 45 miles per hour. With the timing of the cold front 
currently set to occur during the morning time frame, this means 
that peak winds will also occur during the morning, decreasing as 
the day continues and the front exits further east. 

After the departure of the cold front, the region is set to cool 
down closer to normal. 850mb temperatures will take a drastic drop 
from the upper teens Celsius to the positive 2-5 Celsius range, just 
below the median value for this time of year. Naturally, high 
temperatures just below late October normals can be expected Sunday 
and into next week (highs in the upper 40s to low 50s). An upper-
level low will move up into the region at the start of next week, 
providing additional chances for precipitation. From Sunday through 
Tuesday morning, latest probabilities for half an inch of 
accumulation sit at around 20-50%, increasing as you move from north 
to south. Heaviest precipitation is currently expected late Sunday 
into early Monday. During that time frame, there is some signal for 
portions of north central South Dakota to see sub-freezing 
temperatures. Model profiles also show potential for saturation in 
the DGZ and sub-freezing temperatures through the profile, creating 
some chances for the first flurries of the season over north central 
South Dakota Monday morning. The main caveat to this scenario is 
that with cloud cover expected to be present, temperatures are most 
likely a bit too low. The upper percentiles that temperatures may 
trend towards are above freezing, so perhaps the flurries will hold 
off for the time being. Either way, there is still a fair degree of 
spread and uncertainty still with this system, and there is plenty 
of time for timing, precip amounts, and precip type to come further 
into focus.
